coverage.assessment: Several cuts in the revision leave conclusions without their setups. The Gibbs wonder has no payoff. The German detour lacks the hope that the later 'sigh of relief' answers. Adams's disclaimer of responsibility has lost its grounds.

Two pronouns lose their anchors. 'He sailed for Europe' now follows Pumpelly and Gibbs, and 'expect it' in paragraph 2 has no clear object. The oyster in paragraph 23 enters without the shell comparison.
There is no dialogue. Quotations stay marked and attributed, except that the Poincare unity quote has lost its in-paragraph attribution (see F4).

Pruning of qualifiers weakens the framing. The crystal objection was framed as 'some doubt of its bearing' but now reads as a flat assertion. The first draft had already dropped 'As far as one ventured to interpret actual science', though 'If this view was correct' still keeps the final claim conditional.
The 310 comparison and the cannon-ball passage foreshadow the Dynamic Theory without explaining it. Balfour's 1904 aside and the age line are both retained.

The revision strips the 'perpetual' anaphora, the 'words are slippery and thought is viscous' aphorism and the eighteenth-century-education deflation. The fabulist sentence is left with an orphan dash ('how--after').
Three thematic threads are weakened: ignorance as method, man-made order echoing Pearson's 'dream of man', and the woman's ordered shell contrasted with science's raft.
All three dependencies survive at both endpoints in this run's drafts.

strengths: All eight verbatim targets survive in context, including the one-line 'Suddenly, in 1900, science raised its head and denied.' paragraph.
Pearson's quotations keep their sequence from the deep-sea fish through 'cannot infer' to 'chaos', ending on Adams's epigram 'Chaos was the law of nature; Order was the dream of man.'
The raft passage keeps both the 310 analogy and Adams's personal place 'on the raft'.
The Truth genealogy and Balfour's 'convenience was truth' preserve the Poincare-derived irony.
The ignorance catalogue is trimmed to about the planned half-dozen items while keeping the firefly simile and the 'we are probably incapable of discovering' dictum.
summary: The revision keeps the chapter's spine. All eight verbatim lines, the Pearson, Haeckel, Mach, Poincare and physicists quotations, the raft and 310 passage, the Truth genealogy, Balfour's dating, the reduced Lucretius and the final alternative all survive. The second pass, however, removes many of the small hinge sentences that the first draft had kept. These losses include: the Gibbs setup and its payoff; the historian's 'direction only' stance; the hope that motivates the German detour; Poincare's need for unity and Adams's rebuttal to him; the 'admission of ignorance' and Zeno's continuity gloss; the 'perpetual' series; the man-made-truth and raft contrasts in the oyster passage; and Adams's grounds for disclaiming responsibility. No single cut breaks the chapter, but together they flatten the argument's connective tissue and Adams's ironic voice. All planned dependencies remain intact.
